38532: In Christ the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily; believers have been filled, forgiven and freed from the powers.
38534: Food rules, festivals, visions and ascetic regulations are shadows that cannot restrain the flesh.
38536: Set minds on things above, put off the old self and put on compassion, forgiveness and love.
38538: The household code, prayer and wise conduct toward outsiders, then greetings and the letter swap with Laodicea.
38539: Christ is all, and you are complete in him
38554: Christ is all and in all
38559: Completeness. All of God's fullness dwells in Christ, and believers are 'filled' in him, so nothing needs adding.
38561: A visible representation. Christ is the image of the invisible God, and believers are renewed after the image of their creator, recalling Genesis 1:27.
38563: The heir with highest rank, and the first to rise from the dead; not 'first created'.
38565: Basic elements of the world or of teaching, possibly the spiritual forces associated with them. Believers have died with Christ to them.
38566: God's long-hidden purpose now revealed: 'Christ in you (Gentiles), the hope of glory'.
38567: Written at the same time and carried with Colossians; Onesimus, Philemon's slave, travels with Tychicus.
38568: Ephesians shares much of Colossians' structure and wording, especially on the household and new life.
38569: Wisdom present with God at creation lies behind Christ as the one through whom all things were made.
38570: Image, creation and new humanity recall Genesis 1.
38571: Revelation's letter to nearby Laodicea shows the later state of a neighbouring church.
38572: John's prologue presents a similar high Christology: the Word through whom all things were made.
38573: Colossians offers one of the New Testament's highest views of Christ. Everything in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, was created 'through him and for him', he holds all things together, and God was pleased to reconcile all things to himself through him, 'making peace by the blood of his cross' (Col 1:16-20). In him 'the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily' (Col 2:9). Christian creeds draw heavily on these verses. Their roots in Jewish Wisdom tradition show early Jewish believers expressing Jesus' identity with the categories Israel already had for God's presence and activity in creation.
38574: Colossians 2:16-17 as proof that God abolished the Sabbath for everyone
38575: Colossians 2:16-17 shows that the Sabbath and food laws were done away with at the cross; Jewish practice is now obsolete and observing it is legalism.
38576: The verse tells Gentile believers not to let anyone 'judge' them over these things. James Dunn argues the pressure came from local Jews whose practices attracted Gentile believers; 'Paul within Judaism' readers note that the letter does not address Jewish believers or tell them to stop. 'Shadow' and 'substance' contrast a pointer with what it points to, not something evil with something good. The real target is a whole system of ascetic rules and visionary experiences that made Christ seem insufficient.
38577: Douglas Moo and other evangelical commentators maintain that Paul does teach that the Mosaic calendar and food laws, as covenant obligations, have reached their fulfilment in Christ and are not binding on believers, which fits Rom 14:5-6. But most agree this does not make observance sinful or Judaism legalistic, and Christian traditions differ on whether a weekly day of rest remains a creation principle (Sabbatarians and many Reformed) or not.
38578: The passage is about freedom from being judged, so it should not become a tool for judging others, either those who keep Jewish customs or those who do not.
38579: 'Firstborn of all creation' as meaning Christ was created
38580: Some groups (for example Jehovah's Witnesses, following the ancient Arians) read 'firstborn of all creation' as meaning Christ was the first thing God made. Some ordinary readers also find the phrase confusing.
38581: In the Old Testament 'firstborn' marks rank and inheritance: Israel is God's firstborn (Exod 4:22), and God makes David 'firstborn, highest of the kings of the earth' though he was the youngest son (Ps 89:27). The next verse explains why Christ is firstborn: 'for by him all things were created' (Col 1:16), placing him on the Creator's side.
38582: Evangelical, Catholic and Orthodox scholars agree on this; it is the classic Nicene reading defended since Athanasius. The disagreement is between traditions, not mainly among academic commentators, who largely agree that rank is meant.
38583: The passage is central to belief in Christ's divinity and to his authority over every spiritual power feared by the Colossians.
38584: A church tempted by spiritual elitism, special experiences and strict rules was told that it already had everything in Christ, that the powers it feared were defeated, and that holiness comes from union with the risen Christ, not from harsh discipline of the body.
38585: Colossians speaks to anyone told that faith in Christ needs an extra technique, secret knowledge, diet, experience or spiritual hierarchy to be complete. It also offers a vision of Christ as Lord over creation, science and culture, and a new humanity where ethnic and social labels lose their power to rank.
38586: In what is probably the oldest Christian writing we have, Paul encourages new believers who are suffering for having turned from idols, and comforts them that their dead will rise to meet the Lord at his coming.
38588: The three missionaries who founded the church (Acts 17:1-9). Paul is the main voice ('I, Paul', 1 Thess 2:18), but the letter speaks as 'we' throughout, reflecting a team.
38589: Undisputed. The vivid, specific memories of the founding visit, the plans and travels of Timothy (1 Thess 3:1-6) and the early, simple theology fit Paul around 50. A minority view treats 1 Thess 2:14-16 as a later insertion, but most scholars accept it as Paul's.
38590: Paul had gone on from Thessalonica to Berea and Athens (1 Thess 3:1); Timothy rejoined him, and Acts places the reunion with Silas and Timothy in Corinth (Acts 18:5).
38591: A young, mostly Gentile church of manual workers and their households
38593: Paul had been forced out after only a few weeks or months (Acts 17:5-10). The converts faced hostility from their own fellow citizens (1 Thess 2:14), Paul worried that persecution had crushed their faith, and some members had died, raising the fear that they would miss the Lord's coming (1 Thess 4:13).
38594: Thessalonica, having backed Antony and Octavian at Philippi, is rewarded as a 'free city' with its own magistrates, the politarchs.
38595: Claudius becomes emperor; coins and inscriptions in Thessalonica honour the emperors and the goddess Roma.
38596: Claudius expels Jews from Rome (date from Orosius, debated).
38597: Paul, Silas and Timothy found the church in Thessalonica, then flee to Berea (approximate date).
38598: Paul writes 1 Thessalonians from Corinth, about the time Gallio arrives as proconsul.
38599:
Thessalonica (modern Thessaloniki) was the largest city in Macedonia and the seat of the Roman governor, a port on the Via Egnatia. It was a 'free city', governed by its own officials called politarchs. Acts uses exactly this title (Acts 17:6, Acts 17:8), and more than thirty inscriptions with it have been found, one of the small details that support Luke's accuracy. The city's prosperity depended on loyalty to Rome; it had temples to Roma and the emperors, and coins hailing Julius Caesar as a god.

According to Acts, Paul preached in the synagogue for three Sabbaths and won some Jews, many God-fearing Greeks and leading women (Acts 17:1-4). Opponents dragged his host Jason before the politarchs, charging that the missionaries defied 'the decrees of Caesar, saying there is another king, Jesus' (Acts 17:7). The letter itself says the converts 'turned to God from idols' (1 Thess 1:9), which suggests that most were Gentiles. Giving up the city's gods was not a private choice; it could mean losing work in trade guilds, alienating family and seeming disloyal to the city's divine protectors. That is the 'affliction' they suffered.

Paul writes as a worried parent. He compares himself to a nursing mother and a father (1 Thess 2:7, 1 Thess 2:11), defends himself against any suggestion that he was a travelling preacher out for money or flattery (1 Thess 2:3-6), and pours out relief at Timothy's good report (1 Thess 3:6-10). Then he answers a practical pastoral problem: some believers had died, and the church grieved as if they had lost their share in the coming kingdom. Paul's answer, with its trumpet, archangel and meeting in the air, is the basis of much later teaching about the end, but here its purpose is comfort (1 Thess 4:18).
38601: City life revolved around worship of many gods at festivals, guild dinners and civic events. Converts who stopped were seen as atheists and bad citizens, and their neighbours could blame them for any misfortune.
38603: Cities were full of travelling speakers, some sincere, some charlatans seeking money and admiration. Paul distances himself from them: he worked night and day so as not to burden anyone.
38605: Parousia ('presence, arrival') was used for a ruler's official visit to a city. Citizens went out to meet (apantēsis) him and escorted him back in. Many scholars see this picture in 1 Thess 4:15-17; others think the word means simply 'meeting'.
38607: Roman propaganda celebrated the peace and safety brought by Rome. Many scholars hear an echo of such slogans in 1 Thess 5:3; others doubt a specific slogan is meant.
38609: The elite despised manual labour, but the converts were mostly artisans. Paul urges them to live quietly and work so as to win outsiders' respect and not depend on patrons.
38611: Paul asks that the letter be read to all the brothers and sisters, and that they greet each other with a holy kiss, a family greeting that marked them as kin.
38612:
Though written to former pagans, 1 Thessalonians uses the language of Israel. These Gentiles are 'beloved by God' and 'chosen' (1 Thess 1:4), words used of Israel in Deuteronomy. They have turned 'to serve a living and true God', the Jewish description of conversion from idols (compare Jer 10:10). They are called to 'holiness' and to avoid sexual immorality 'like the Gentiles who do not know God' (1 Thess 4:5), which shows that Paul thinks of them as no longer belonging to 'the Gentiles' in the old sense, even though they are not Jews. Paula Fredriksen calls such people 'ex-pagan pagans'.

The hope Paul offers is Jewish apocalyptic hope: the 'day of the Lord' of the prophets (Amos 5:18, Joel 2:31), the resurrection of the dead (Dan 12:2), the trumpet (Isa 27:13) and the Lord coming with his holy ones (Zech 14:5). Paul simply identifies 'the Lord' of that hope as Jesus.

One passage has caused deep pain: 1 Thess 2:14-16, which speaks of 'the Jews, who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets' and on whom 'wrath has come at last'. Some scholars (Birger Pearson) think it is a later insertion written after 70. Most accept it as Paul's but read it as an intra-Jewish prophetic polemic, like the prophets' denunciations of their own people, aimed at particular Judean opponents of the mission, not at the Jewish people as a whole. The Greek has no comma, and some translators argue the phrase should read 'the Judeans who...' rather than 'the Jews, who...', restricting it. Paul's later word that God has not rejected his people (Rom 11:1-2) should be read alongside it.
38614: The gospel came with power, and their turn from idols is known throughout Macedonia and Achaia.
38616: Paul recalls his gentle, unpaid, parent-like ministry and their suffering for the word.
38618: Kept away, he sent Timothy, whose good news brought joy; he prays to see them again.
38620: Avoid sexual immorality, love each other more and more, and work quietly.
38622: Do not grieve without hope: the dead in Christ rise first, and all will meet the Lord together.
38624: The day comes like a thief, so stay awake, armed with faith, love and the hope of salvation.
38626: Respect leaders, help the weak, rejoice, pray, test prophecy; may God sanctify you completely.
38627: Hope for a suffering young church
38648: The royal arrival of Jesus as Lord. Paul uses it four times in this short letter.
38650: Pressure, distress, persecution: the social cost of the converts' new faith.
38651: Trust and steadfast loyalty. Timothy's report is about their pistis holding firm under pressure.
38653: Being set apart for God, worked out in concrete sexual and social ethics.
38654: 'The church of the Thessalonians in God the Father': a civic word for assembly, now used for God's gathered people.
38655: Acts 17 tells of the founding, the riot, Jason and the politarchs.
38656: The follow-up letter corrects confusion about the day of the Lord and idleness.
38657: The resurrection hope and the coming of the Lord build on Daniel's vision of the dead awakening and the Son of Man coming with the clouds.
38658: Jesus' sayings about the thief in the night and the trumpet gathering of the elect seem to lie behind Paul's teaching.
38659: 1 Corinthians 15 develops the resurrection at the last trumpet in more detail.
38660: Here Jesus is 'the Lord' who died and rose (1 Thess 4:14), who 'delivers us from the wrath to come' (1 Thess 1:10), and who will come from heaven with the holy ones. Paul applies to Jesus the Old Testament 'day of the LORD' and the prophets' hope of God coming with his holy ones (Zech 14:5, 1 Thess 3:13). Writing within about twenty years of the crucifixion, Paul prays to Jesus alongside God the Father (1 Thess 3:11), evidence of very early devotion to Jesus within a Jewish monotheistic framework. Jewish readers can see in the letter a Jewish messianic movement offering Gentiles a share in Israel's end-time hope.
38661: 1 Thessalonians 4:17 as a secret, pre-tribulation rapture
38662: 1 Thess 4:16-17 describes the rapture: Christ will come secretly for his church, believers will vanish to heaven, and the world will then go through a seven-year tribulation before Christ returns visibly to reign. This framework, popularised by J. N. Darby in the 1830s, the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) and the Left Behind novels, is taught in many evangelical churches.
38663: The passage is meant to comfort grieving believers that their dead will not miss out. Nothing in it is secret: there is a shout, an archangel's voice and God's trumpet. Many scholars (N. T. Wright, Ben Witherington, Gene Green) argue that apantēsis, 'meeting', evokes citizens going out to greet an arriving ruler and escorting him back to the city, so believers rise to meet Christ and return with him to a renewed earth. The 'caught up' language may also echo Elijah's ascent and Daniel's clouds. Paul says nothing here about a seven-year tribulation.
38664: Pretribulational scholars such as John Walvoord and Thomas Ice argue that the meeting in the air removes believers from the earth before God's wrath (1 Thess 1:10, 1 Thess 5:9), that the apantēsis 'escort' sense is overstated (the word simply means 'meeting', and context decides), and that the church and Israel have distinct roles in the end-time programme. Other evangelicals, such as Robert Gundry (post-tribulational) and George Ladd (historic premillennial), reject a separate secret coming while accepting a literal meeting in the air. Evangelicals are divided; this is a genuine debate, not only a popular misreading. See /debates/rapture.
38665: The rapture framework shapes how many believers think about current events, Israel, and the future of the earth. Paul's own focus is hope for the dead and a call to steady, holy living.
38666: 1 Thessalonians 2:14-16 as a condemnation of the Jewish people
38667: The Jews killed Jesus and the prophets and are under God's wrath; this passage has been quoted in sermons and tracts as Scripture's verdict on the Jewish people.
38668: Paul, himself a Jew, is comparing the Gentile converts' suffering from their own compatriots with the suffering of the Judean churches from theirs. The prophetic charge of killing the prophets is a stock Jewish self-critique (Neh 9:26). Scholars such as Jeffrey Weima, Abraham Malherbe and the Jewish Annotated New Testament contributors read it as targeted polemic against particular Judean opponents of the mission, not all Jews. Some (Birger Pearson) think it is a post-70 interpolation.
38669: Evangelical commentators (Weima, Gene Green, Gordon Fee) defend authenticity and agree that the passage must not be used for anti-Jewish purposes, reading it in line with Romans 9-11. There is scholarly disagreement on authenticity, but near-universal agreement that it is not a blanket condemnation.
38670: This text was misused in the history of Christian antisemitism. Reading it as Paul's own intra-Jewish prophetic speech, beside Romans 11, guards against that.
38671: New believers who had paid a social price for leaving their gods learned that their faith was real, that their founder loved them, and that death would not separate them from Christ or from each other.
38672: 1 Thessalonians gives Christians language for grief with hope at funerals (1 Thess 4:13-14), a model of pastoral care that is gentle and unpaid, and a call to steady, ordinary, holy living instead of speculation about dates.
38673: A short letter to steady a persecuted church shaken by a claim that the day of the Lord had already come: God will judge justly, certain events must come first, so stand firm and keep working.
38675: Presented as the same team as 1 Thessalonians, writing a few months later. If pseudonymous, a later Paulinist imitated 1 Thessalonians to correct end-time enthusiasm in the name of Paul.
38676: The letter claims Paul and ends with his own signature as 'the sign of genuineness in every letter' (2 Thess 3:17). Doubters (Wolfgang Trilling, Maarten Menken) note that much of its wording copies 1 Thessalonians while its tone is cooler and its end-time scheme (signs first) seems different. Defenders (Abraham Malherbe, Jeffrey Weima, Gordon Fee) answer that a follow-up letter written soon after would naturally repeat phrases, and that the difference is a response to a new misunderstanding. Scholarly opinion is divided.
38678: If Pauline, it was written from Corinth during the same stay as 1 Thessalonians, since Silas and Timothy are still with Paul (2 Thess 1:1, Acts 18:5). If pseudonymous, the place is unknown.
38680: Persecution had intensified (2 Thess 1:4-6). Someone, by 'a spirit or a spoken word, or a letter seeming to be from us', had claimed that the day of the Lord had already arrived (2 Thess 2:2). Some members had stopped working and were living off others (2 Thess 3:6-12), perhaps because they thought the end had come, perhaps because they were relying on the church's generosity.
38681: Emperor Gaius (Caligula) orders his statue to be set up in the Jerusalem temple; the order is delayed and then cancelled at his death in 41. Many think this crisis shaped expectations of a ruler who would sit in God's temple.
38682: Probable date of 2 Thessalonians if written by Paul a few months after the first letter.
38683: The Jewish revolt against Rome begins.
38684: Roman destruction of the Jerusalem temple; a post-Pauline 2 Thessalonians would be written after this.
38685:
The situation behind 2 Thessalonians is a church under pressure from outside and confused from inside. The believers were enduring 'persecutions and afflictions' that Paul could boast of to other churches (2 Thess 1:4). Into that pain came a teaching that 'the day of the Lord has come'. It is not clear what this meant: perhaps that the final judgement had begun in their sufferings, perhaps a spiritualised idea that the resurrection had already happened (compare 2 Tim 2:18). It was apparently backed by a prophecy or a letter claiming Paul's authority, which is why Paul signs this one so emphatically.

Paul's reply refers back to his oral teaching (2 Thess 2:5): before the day comes, there will be a 'rebellion' (apostasia) and the revealing of 'the man of lawlessness', who exalts himself and takes his seat in God's temple. Something or someone is 'restraining' him now (2 Thess 2:6-7). The first readers knew what Paul meant; later readers do not. Proposed identifications of the restrainer include the Roman empire and its law (the most common ancient view, found in Tertullian), the preaching of the gospel, the Holy Spirit or the church, God himself, or an angel such as Michael (Dan 12:1). The lawless figure echoes Daniel's description of Antiochus IV, who desecrated the temple in 167 BC (Dan 11:36), and the more recent attempt by Caligula to place his statue in the Jerusalem temple in 40.

The third issue, the 'disorderly' (ataktoi) who would not work, may reflect both end-time excitement and the patronage system: some poorer members may have attached themselves to wealthier believers as clients. Paul's 'if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat' (2 Thess 3:10) points back to his own example of working to support himself.
38687: Letters could be forged, and senders authenticated them with a handwritten closing. 2 Thessalonians warns against a letter 'as if from us' and ends with Paul's own hand.
38689: In an honour culture, the shamed would expect vindication. Paul assures the persecuted that God will repay affliction and grant them rest, and that God's honour will be shown in them.
38691: Rulers who claimed divine honours were part of the political landscape, from Antiochus IV to Caligula. The man of lawlessness who claims to be God fits this pattern.
38693: Poorer citizens often survived as clients of patrons, owing them public support in return for handouts. Paul wants believers to work and not become dependent, while not tiring of doing good to those in real need.
38695: Paul's teaching was passed on both orally and in letters (paradosis, 'traditions'). The church is to hold fast to both.
